Next priority: independent validation of H6 when allowed, unless batch/marker checks reveal technical confounding. SMARCA2 batch caveat: H50 small opposite interaction R32 -0.051 [-0.095,-0.007], active; analyze H58 batch_a main effect. New proposals: marker-D controls for WRN, SMARCA2, NFE2L2, USP7 and WRN batch_b main effect. Next analyze should prioritize H57/H58, new marker-D controls, H42/H47, H56, H55, and EGFR/KRAS refinements if slots allow. Negative associations: KRAS mutation/KRAS, STK11/KRAS, BRAF V600E/BRAF, ERBB2 amp/ERBB2, TP53/MDM2, PIK3CA/STAT3, MYC/DHX9/RPL11/POLR2A, BRCA2/KIF18A, ARID1A overall/SMARCA2. EGFR remains unresolved and should not be accepted without robust clinically meaningful stratum evidence and preferably validation. All accepted claims are dataset associations, not causal or external-generalizable claims.","latest_stage_narratives":{"explore":"Current state: four very large associations are accepted, and three are independently validated in some form: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency is accepted but remains the main large claim without validation. The next exploratory set is therefore weighted toward WRN robustness, independence of co-mutational context for the accepted effects, specificity controls, and a few biologically motivated broad tests that could still clear the clinically meaningful 10% relative benchmark.  \n\nFor WRN, I register refinements asking whether the MSI-high association survives in higher-mutation-burden tumors, in higher-Cas9-activity screens, and in KRAS-wild-type tumors. These address plausible alternatives: that the WRN effect is driven by global hypermutation rather than MSI specifically; that it is an artifact of variable CRISPR quality; or that it is concentrated in a common co-mutational lineage. They complement the pending batch and marker-D controls. If these remain large and controls remain null, they will strengthen the case for independent validation of H6.  \n\nFor SMARCA2, I test SMARCA4 loss among TP53-wild-type tumors to determine whether the effect is not simply entangled with TP53 co-loss. I also add a cross-outcome specificity control: SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A dependency. Because POLR2A is not mechanistically tied to SMARCA4, a near-null result would support outcome-specific paralog dependence, whereas a large effect would raise concern about broader screen or cohort structure affecting SMARCA2.  \n\nFor the validated reversal effects, I test TP53-loss/USP7 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors. KRAS co-mutation is common in lung adenocarcinoma, and these tests ask whether the large associations remain when removing a frequent co-mutational driver context. I also add marker-F controls for USP7 and NFE2L2 because marker-E and marker-D controls are already registered or pending; a null marker-F result would complete a role-free marker control set for these outcomes.  \n\nEGFR amplification remains the most interesting unresolved oncogene match. Its overall point estimate is directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency but small and uncertain. I register an oncogene-exclusive adenocarcinoma context, excluding KRAS mutation, BRAF V600E, and ERBB2 amplification. If EGFR dependency is driven by a cleaner driver-exclusive population, this refinement could clarify whether the small signal becomes clinically meaningful and worth validation.  \n\nFinally, KRAS mutation itself was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency, but pathway dependence may be shaped by upstream regulators. NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling, so I register NF1 loss versus both KRAS and RIT1 dependency. These are exploratory tests of pathway-level dependence after direct KRAS-mutation and STK11-loss tests were not significant. All proposed comparisons remain dataset-specific association tests; none imply causality or external generalizability.","analyze":"The selected 12 analyses are aimed first at the central remaining decision problem: whether the accepted MSI-high/WRN association is robust enough to justify independent validation. H6 currently has an enormous signed effect, but its technical and co-factor robustness is incomplete: the non-Avana stratum was unestimable, the batch_a interaction was inconclusive, and I have not yet tested direct batch main effects, Cas9-quality or mutation-burden strata, KRAS-wild-type context, or marker-D specificity. Therefore I run WRN batch_a and batch_b main effects (H57, H63), high-mutation-burden and high-Cas9-activity strata (H64, H65), KRAS-wild-type context (H66), and the marker-D control (H59). If these remain large, clinically meaningful, and marker-D is near null, the WRN association will look much stronger than the earlier partial checks and I will consider validating H6 in the next appraise. If marker-D or one of the technical/co-factor strata shows a large contradictory or attenuating effect, I will defer validation and prioritize confounding explanations.  \n\nThe second block completes marker-D controls for the other accepted very large associations: SMARCA2, NFE2L2, and USP7 (H60, H61, H62). Because research marker D has no assigned biology, a large association would raise concern that the huge dependency-score differences reflect broad correlated cohort or technical structure rather than biomarker-specific association. Near-null marker-D results would strengthen specificity of the accepted effects, especially WRN and SMARCA2.  \n\nI also run H58, the SMARCA4-loss main effect within batch_a, because H50 showed a small opposite batch interaction (R32 -0.051 [-0.095,-0.007]) for SMARCA2. Although H7 is validated and closed, this quantifies whether the effect remains large inside the batch associated with the caveat. H67 tests SMARCA4 loss among TP53-wild-type tumors, checking that the SMARCA2 effect is not entangled with frequent TP53 co-loss. Finally, H71 is a broad unresolved candidate: EGFR amplification in driver-exclusive adenocarcinoma, excluding KRAS mutation, BRAF V600E, and ERBB2 amplification. EGFR remains unresolved overall, but if a cleaner driver-exclusive stratum shows a clinically meaningful and reasonably precise effect, it would justify follow-up. These are dataset-specific association tests; no causal or external-generalizability claim is being advanced.","appraise":"The new evidence is highly favorable to the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 association and generally reassuring for specificity. H44 shows a very large non-Avana-library effect: R28 is +0.801 signed, interval +0.748 to +0.853, with valid cell sizes 61 and 174. Because H44's direction is -1, this corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference, i.e. much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in SMARCA4-loss tumors outside the dominant Avana stratum. This is far above the 10% relative benchmark and much larger than any observed control effect. H36 is similarly informative: R35 is +0.777 signed, interval +0.756 to +0.798, in ARID1A-wild-type tumors. This supports the specificity of SMARCA4 loss rather than generic BAF-complex loss, and H37 is null: R36 is -0.003, interval -0.025 to +0.019, arguing against ARID1A loss independently predicting stronger SMARCA2 dependency in SMARCA4-wild-type tumors. H46, H51, and H52 are marker controls; R30, R33, and R34 are all near null and far from the large biomarker effects, which reduces concern that these very large associations are driven by nonspecific role-free marker association. H45 confirms that the validated KEAP1/NFE2L2 reversal is also large in non-Avana samples: R29 is +0.794, interval +0.746 to +0.842.\n\nThe WRN robustness picture is less complete. H43 failed because the non-Avana MSI-high exposed cell had only 10 observations, so it provides no usable evidence and remains unresolved/deferred. H49 WRN batch_a interaction is not decisive: R31 is +0.048 signed, interval -0.019 to +0.115. Directionally it is compatible with a somewhat stronger association in batch_a, but the interval includes zero and admits both small and clinically large effects, so it cannot close the technical question. H50 for SMARCA2 is statistically significant but in the opposite direction to the hypothesized signed claim: R32 is -0.051 signed, interval -0.095 to -0.007. This corresponds to a modestly weaker raw association in batch_a relative to its complement. I reject the specific H50 direction, but I keep it active as a small technical caveat because the interval is not negligible and it is the one result suggesting possible screen-batch heterogeneity for SMARCA2. The main effect is so large, and the non-Avana and ARID1A-wild-type estimates are so consistent, that this small opposite interaction does not currently outweigh the association; however, I registered batch-specific main-effect proposals to quantify whether the SMARCA4 effect remains large within batch_a itself.\n\nThe EGFR signal remains unresolved. H53 is directionally supportive of stronger EGFR dependency with EGFR amplification in TP53-loss tumors (R37 +0.025, interval -0.031 to +0.080), but the point estimate is borderline relative to the 10% benchmark and the interval is wide because of smaller cells. H54 STK11 loss is null for KRAS dependency. Given that H7 now has enormous main discovery evidence, Avana robustness, non-Avana robustness, ARID1A-specificity, and null marker controls, I request independent validation of H7 rather than H6. H6 remains active, but its non-Avana stratum could not be estimated and its batch interaction remains underpowered; H7 is currently the most mature unvalidated large association. The request is an independent replication of an association in this dataset, not a test of causality or generalizability beyond the supplied system.","synthesize":"The newly delivered validation evidence is decisive for the SMARCA4-loss association with SMARCA2 dependency and confirms the previously accepted response deadline for TP53 loss with USP7 dependency. H7 had a very large discovery effect, R7 +0.784 [0.765, 0.803], and its independent validation, R39 +0.801 [0.771, 0.830], is concordant and still enormous after accounting for the maximum number of validation comparisons. Because H7 has direction -1, these positive signed estimates correspond to raw exposed-minus-comparator differences that are strongly negative, i.e. SMARCA4-loss tumors have much stronger, more negative SMARCA2 dependency. The effect is far above the 10% clinical-significance benchmark and is many standard deviations relative to the SMARCA2 dependency distribution. I therefore accept H7 as a supported association in this dataset and close its main investigation. This remains an association, not proof of causality or generalizability beyond the supplied data.\n\nH28 asks whether the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 association is present in the dominant Avana library stratum. Discovery R19 was +0.776 [0.753, 0.799], and validation R40 was +0.796 [0.761, 0.831]. These are essentially identical in magnitude and both are clinically enormous. I therefore accept and close H28 as an assay-stratum robustness check. Together with H44, which was large in non-Avana samples, and H36, which was large in ARID1A-wild-type tumors, this argues that the SMARCA4 effect is not confined to one library stratum or to co-loss with ARID1A. H46 and H52 marker controls were near null, and H37 showed no ARID1A-loss effect in SMARCA4-wild-type tumors. This specificity pattern reduces concern that the SMARCA2 result is a generic BAF-complex or role-free-marker artifact. The remaining SMARCA2 caveat is H50: R32 is a small interaction in the opposite direction to the hypothesized signed main-effect direction, -0.051 [-0.095, -0.007]. It is much smaller than the main effect, but I keep it active and retain H58 to quantify the batch_a main effect directly.\n\nThe H11 response deadline is satisfied. Discovery R11 was +0.802 [0.782, 0.822], and validation R13 was +0.800 [0.769, 0.832]. With direction +1, this means TP53-loss tumors have raw positive exposed-minus-comparator differences, i.e. weaker USP7 dependency. The two estimates are nearly identical, both intervals are far from zero, and the effect is much larger than the 10% benchmark. I reaffirm H11 as accepted and closed. This contrasts with H5, where TP53 loss was not associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, supporting that the USP7 result is not merely a generic TP53-loss dependency effect.\n\nThe KEAP1/NFE2L2 reversal remains accepted: H17 has discovery and validation evidence showing much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss tumors, while the original synthetic-lethal direction in H8 is rejected. Thus the dataset currently supports four very large biomarker-dependency associations: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency. The first three are now independently validated in some form, while the fourth remains accepted but not yet independently validated.\n\nH6 remains the most important unresolved large claim. It has an enormous discovery effect, R6 +0.790 [0.760, 0.819], and strong Avana-stratum support, R18 +0.813 [0.778, 0.847]. Marker-E and marker-F controls were null, which supports specificity. To prepare that decision, I registered batch_b WRN robustness and marker-D controls for WRN and SMARCA2, as well as marker-D controls for the two validated reversal effects. record.narrative:
The new WRN evidence strongly supports the already accepted MSI-high association and makes independent validation the highest-value next test. For H57, the signed batch_a main effect is R41 = +0.824 [0.766, 0.882]; because the hypothesis direction is -1, this corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference, i.e. MSI-high tumors in batch_a have much stronger WRN dependency. H63 gives a similarly large batch_b main effect, R42 = +0.789 [0.726, 0.852]. These are not small technical artifacts: they are on the order of three standard deviations of the WRN score distribution and far exceed the 10% clinical-significance benchmark under any sensible scale. H64 shows that restricting to high mutation burden does not collapse the effect, R43 = +0.775 [0.737, 0.812], which argues against a simple explanation in which MSI-high is only a proxy for global hypermutation. H65 shows that restricting to higher Cas9 activity also leaves the effect very large, R44 = +0.776 [0.728, 0.824], reducing concern that this is an artifact of weak CRISPR performance, although Cas9 activity is missing for part of the dataset and selection into measured high-activity screens cannot be fully ruled out. H66 shows that the effect is not confined to KRAS-mutant co-mutational context, R45 = +0.792 [0.759, 0.825] in KRAS-wild-type tumors. Taken with the overall estimate R6 = +0.790 and the Avana stratum R18 = +0.813, the WRN result is highly internally robust except that the non-Avana WRN stratum remains unestimable due to only 10 exposed observations in R27.  

The role-free marker-D controls are reassuring for specificity. H59 gives R46 = +0.012 [-0.011, 0.035], H60 gives R47 = +0.002 [-0.030, 0.035], H61 gives R48 = -0.001 [-0.032, 0.031], and H62 gives R49 = +0.005 [-0.027, 0.038]. These are near null and several orders smaller than the biomarker associations. I cannot exclude a very small marker-D association, but the evidence does not support marker-D as a driver of the huge WRN, SMARCA2, NFE2L2, or USP7 effects, and these controls argue against a generic role-free-marker or broad cohort-structure explanation. I therefore reject the marker-D association hypotheses and close these controls.  

The SMARCA2 batch caveat is now resolved as a technical caveat rather than a substantive challenge. H58 gives the batch_a main effect of SMARCA4 loss on SMARCA2 as R50 = +0.747 [0.709, 0.785], again enormous. This means that although the small batch_a interaction in R32 was opposite the main-effect direction, the effect within batch_a itself remains very large. I therefore close H50. H67 similarly shows that SMARCA4 loss remains strongly associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency among TP53-wild-type tumors, R51 = +0.787 [0.766, 0.809], reducing concern that the SMARCA2 result is merely entangled with TP53 co-loss.  

The EGFR driver-exclusive refinement remains unresolved. H71 gives R52 = +0.021 [-0.017, 0.060]. The direction is consistent with stronger EGFR dependency, but the point estimate is small, the interval includes both null and modestly larger effects, and the exposed cell is modest. This is not enough to accept an EGFR dependency association. Because many EGFR stratum tests are small and uncertain, I defer H71 and do not request validation for EGFR.  

Given that WRN now has a very large overall effect, library-stratum support, both largest batch main effects, high-mutation-burden support, high-Cas9 support, KRAS-wild-type support, and null role-free marker controls, the main remaining concern is discovery multiplicity and residual confounding. An independent validation split is the best next evidence. I request independent validation of H6. This request is for replication of a dataset association only, not a claim of causality or external generalizability.

MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency is accepted but remains the main large claim without validation. The next exploratory set is therefore weighted toward WRN robustness, independence of co-mutational context for the accepted effects, specificity controls, and a few biologically motivated broad tests that could still clear the clinically meaningful 10% relative benchmark.  \n\nFor WRN, I register refinements asking whether the MSI-high association survives in higher-mutation-burden tumors, in higher-Cas9-activity screens, and in KRAS-wild-type tumors. These address plausible alternatives: that the WRN effect is driven by global hypermutation rather than MSI specifically; that it is an artifact of variable CRISPR quality; or that it is concentrated in a common co-mutational lineage. They complement the pending batch and marker-D controls. If these remain large and controls remain null, they will strengthen the case for independent validation of H6.  \n\nFor SMARCA2, I test SMARCA4 loss among TP53-wild-type tumors to determine whether the effect is not simply entangled with TP53 co-loss. KRAS co-mutation is common in lung adenocarcinoma, and these tests ask whether the large associations remain when removing a frequent co-mutational driver context. I also add marker-F controls for USP7 and NFE2L2 because marker-E and marker-D controls are already registered or pending; a null marker-F result would complete a role-free marker control set for these outcomes.  \n\nEGFR amplification remains the most interesting unresolved oncogene match. Its overall point estimate is directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency but small and uncertain. I register an oncogene-exclusive adenocarcinoma context, excluding KRAS mutation, BRAF V600E, and ERBB2 amplification. If EGFR dependency is driven by a cleaner driver-exclusive population, this refinement could clarify whether the small signal becomes clinically meaningful and worth validation.  \n\nFinally, KRAS mutation itself was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency, but pathway dependence may be shaped by upstream regulators. NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling, so I register NF1 loss versus both KRAS and RIT1 dependency. These are exploratory tests of pathway-level dependence after direct KRAS-mutation and STK11-loss tests were not significant. All proposed comparisons remain dataset-specific association tests; none imply causality or external generalizability.","analyze":"The selected 12 analyses are aimed first at the central remaining decision problem: whether the accepted MSI-high/WRN association is robust enough to justify independent validation. H6 currently has an enormous signed effect, but its technical and co-factor robustness is incomplete: the non-Avana stratum was unestimable, the batch_a interaction was inconclusive, and I have not yet tested direct batch main effects, Cas9-quality or mutation-burden strata, KRAS-wild-type context, or marker-D specificity. If these remain large, clinically meaningful, and marker-D is near null, the WRN association will look much stronger than the earlier partial checks and I will consider validating H6 in the next appraise. If marker-D or one of the technical/co-factor strata shows a large contradictory or attenuating effect, I will defer validation and prioritize confounding explanations.  \n\nThe second block completes marker-D controls for the other accepted very large associations: SMARCA2, NFE2L2, and USP7 (H60, H61, H62). Because research marker D has no assigned biology, a large association would raise concern that the huge dependency-score differences reflect broad correlated cohort or technical structure rather than biomarker-specific association. Near-null marker-D results would strengthen specificity of the accepted effects, especially WRN and SMARCA2.  \n\nI also run H58, the SMARCA4-loss main effect within batch_a, because H50 showed a small opposite batch interaction (R32 -0.051 [-0.095,-0.007]) for SMARCA2. Although H7 is validated and closed, this quantifies whether the effect remains large inside the batch associated with the caveat. H67 tests SMARCA4 loss among TP53-wild-type tumors, checking that the SMARCA2 effect is not entangled with frequent TP53 co-loss. Finally, H71 is a broad unresolved candidate: EGFR amplification in driver-exclusive adenocarcinoma, excluding KRAS mutation, BRAF V600E, and ERBB2 amplification. EGFR remains unresolved overall, but if a cleaner driver-exclusive stratum shows a clinically meaningful and reasonably precise effect, it would justify follow-up. These are dataset-specific association tests; no causal or external-generalizability claim is being advanced.","appraise":"The new WRN evidence strongly supports the already accepted MSI-high association and makes independent validation the highest-value next test. For H57, the signed batch_a main effect is R41 = +0.824 [0.766, 0.882]; because the hypothesis direction is -1, this corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference, i.e. MSI-high tumors in batch_a have much stronger WRN dependency. H63 gives a similarly large batch_b main effect, R42 = +0.789 [0.726, 0.852]. These are not small technical artifacts: they are on the order of three standard deviations of the WRN score distribution and far exceed the 10% clinical-significance benchmark under any sensible scale. H64 shows that restricting to high mutation burden does not collapse the effect, R43 = +0.775 [0.737, 0.812], which argues against a simple explanation in which MSI-high is only a proxy for global hypermutation. H65 shows that restricting to higher Cas9 activity also leaves the effect very large, R44 = +0.776 [0.728, 0.824], reducing concern that this is an artifact of weak CRISPR performance, although Cas9 activity is missing for part of the dataset and selection into measured high-activity screens cannot be fully ruled out. H66 shows that the effect is not confined to KRAS-mutant co-mutational context, R45 = +0.792 [0.759, 0.825] in KRAS-wild-type tumors. Taken with the overall estimate R6 = +0.790 and the Avana stratum R18 = +0.813, the WRN result is highly internally robust except that the non-Avana WRN stratum remains unestimable due to only 10 exposed observations in R27.  \n\nThe role-free marker-D controls are reassuring for specificity. H59 gives R46 = +0.012 [-0.011, 0.035], H60 gives R47 = +0.002 [-0.030, 0.035], H61 gives R48 = -0.001 [-0.032, 0.031], and H62 gives R49 = +0.005 [-0.027, 0.038]. These are near null and several orders smaller than the biomarker associations. I cannot exclude a very small marker-D association, but the evidence does not support marker-D as a driver of the huge WRN, SMARCA2, NFE2L2, or USP7 effects, and these controls argue against a generic role-free-marker or broad cohort-structure explanation. I therefore reject the marker-D association hypotheses and close these controls.  \n\nThe SMARCA2 batch caveat is now resolved as a technical caveat rather than a substantive challenge. H58 gives the batch_a main effect of SMARCA4 loss on SMARCA2 as R50 = +0.747 [0.709, 0.785], again enormous. This means that although the small batch_a interaction in R32 was opposite the main-effect direction, the effect within batch_a itself remains very large. I therefore close H50. H67 similarly shows that SMARCA4 loss remains strongly associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency among TP53-wild-type tumors, R51 = +0.787 [0.766, 0.809], reducing concern that the SMARCA2 result is merely entangled with TP53 co-loss.  \n\nThe EGFR driver-exclusive refinement remains unresolved. H71 gives R52 = +0.021 [-0.017, 0.060]. The direction is consistent with stronger EGFR dependency, but the point estimate is small, the interval includes both null and modestly larger effects, and the exposed cell is modest. This is not enough to accept an EGFR dependency association. Because many EGFR stratum tests are small and uncertain, I defer H71 and do not request validation for EGFR.  \n\nGiven that WRN now has a very large overall effect, library-stratum support, both largest batch main effects, high-mutation-burden support, high-Cas9 support, KRAS-wild-type support, and null role-free marker controls, the main remaining concern is discovery multiplicity and residual confounding. An independent validation split is the best next evidence. I request independent validation of H6. record.narrative:
The new validation evidence closes the last major open question about the four very large biomarker-dependency associations. For H6, MSI-high versus MSI-low or MSI-negative status in dependency_WRN, independent validation gives R53 = +0.821 [0.766, 0.877] at the stricter validation alpha = 0.00385, with valid cell sizes 125 and 1875. Because H6 has direction -1, this signed positive estimate corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference: MSI-high tumors have substantially more negative WRN dependency scores, i.e. stronger WRN dependency. This is concordant with, and slightly larger than, the discovery estimate R6 = +0.790 [0.760, 0.819]. The validated interval is very far from zero and the magnitude is far above the task's 10% clinically significant difference benchmark; relative to the observed WRN score standard deviation (~0.263), it is roughly a three-standard-deviation effect. Combined with prior internal robustness checks—Avana-library stratum R18 +0.813, batch_a main effect R41 +0.824, batch_b main effect R42 +0.789, high-mutation-burden stratum R43 +0.775, high-Cas9 stratum R44 +0.776, KRAS-wild-type context R45 +0.792, and null marker-D/E/F controls—this supports acceptance of MSI-high as a strong dataset-specific predictor of stronger WRN dependency. I close H6. This remains an association within the supplied dataset; it is not proof of causality or external generalizability. The only residual technical gap is the non-Avana WRN stratum, which could not be estimated because the exposed cell had only 10 observations in R27; however, the independent overall validation substantially mitigates the discovery-multiplicity concern.

The H17 response deadline is satisfied. KEAP1 loss versus no KEAP1 loss in dependency_NFE2L2 remains accepted: discovery R8 = +0.796 [0.776, 0.816] and validation R26 = +0.791 [0.761, 0.821]. Direction +1 means the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is positive, so KEAP1-loss tumors have less negative NFE2L2 scores, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. This is a robust reversal of the initially hypothesized synthetic-lethal direction in H8, which remains rejected. I reaffirm H17 as accepted and closed.

The current supported large-association set is therefore: TP53 loss predicts much weaker USP7 dependency (H11 accepted and validated); KEAP1 loss predicts much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H17 accepted and validated; H8 rejected); SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency (H7 accepted and validated, with multiple stratum and specificity controls); and MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency (H6 now accepted and validated). The SMARCA2 finding is further supported by Avana stratum validation H28, non-Avana discovery R28, ARID1A-wild-type stratum R35, TP53-wild-type stratum R51, and batch_a main effect R50. Role-free marker controls for these outcomes are near null, including marker-D, marker-E, and marker-F tests for WRN and SMARCA2, and marker-D for NFE2L2 and USP7.

The scientifically important negative findings remain dataset-specific and informative: direct matched oncogene-mutation or amplification associations were generally weak or null. KRAS mutation was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency; STK11 loss was not associated with KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E was not associated with BRAF dependency; ERBB2 amplification was not associated with ERBB2 dependency; TP53 loss was not associated with stronger MDM2 dependency; PIK3CA mutation was not associated with stronger STAT3 dependency; MYC amplification was not associated with stronger DHX9, RPL11, or POLR2A dependency; and BRCA2 loss was not associated with stronger KIF18A dependency. ARID1A loss overall was not associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, while SMARCA4 loss was strongly associated, supporting a more SMARCA4-specific paralogous dependence pattern rather than generic BAF-complex loss.

EGFR amplification remains the main unresolved candidate among the clinically motivated oncogene-dependency hypotheses. Several EGFR comparisons are directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency, including the overall estimate R3 +0.025 [-0.000, 0.051], KRAS-wild-type context R22 +0.016 [-0.014, 0.046], TP53-loss context R37 +0.025 [-0.031, 0.080], and driver-exclusive adenocarcinoma refinement R52 +0.021 [-0.017, 0.060]. However, these point estimates are small relative to the accepted huge associations and often underpowered. EGFR should not be accepted unless a more informative stratum or pooled refinement yields a clinically meaningful, reasonably precise effect and preferably independent validation. Other unresolved questions include whether the accepted large effects persist in additional co-mutational or assay-quality strata, especially TP53-loss/USP7 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors, and whether cross-outcome specificity controls such as MSI-high/POLR2A and SMARCA4-loss/POLR2A are near null.

The most informative next analyses are therefore not further validation of the already validated large associations, but (1) completing specificity controls for the large effects, especially cross-outcome controls H76 MSI-high/POLR2A and H68 SMARCA4-loss/POLR2A, plus remaining marker-E/F controls for USP7 and NFE2L2; (2) testing whether the large reversal effects remain in co-mutational contexts H69 TP53-loss/USP7 in KRAS-wild-type tumors and H70 KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors; and (3) resolving EGFR with the registered co-mutation-stratum refinements H14, H38, H48, and related EGFR hypotheses rather than validating the weak overall EGFR signal. These analyses will better distinguish biomarker-specific associations from broader co-mutational structure, technical confounding, or underpowered small effects.

Study instructions:
Investigate diverse, scientifically meaningful comparisons and use previous
results to allocate further investigation. Broad exploration and focused follow-up are both useful
throughout the run. Assess discoveries in this supplied dataset and use independent validation when

Register comparisons, anticipated directions, and initial assessments before requesting analyses.
The controller assigns claim references. For a changed claim, propose a new comparison and link
refinements to the earlier parent claim.
Clinical log_pfs_months is natural log progression-free survival in months, fully observed without
censoring. Dependency scores are continuous; more negative values mean stronger dependency.
Research signatures are constructed standardized assays in arbitrary units. Research markers D, E,
and F are constructed binary assays with no assigned gene, pathway, or clinical role.
A mean_difference is exposed minus comparator within eligibility and subgroup. An interaction
subtracts that comparison in the subgroup complement in the same eligible population.
Use your scientific judgment to assess the size, uncertainty, and importance of each effect
and decide which conclusions the evidence supports. Explain your reasoning in the narrative.
Returned estimates and intervals are ALREADY SIGNED to the indicated hypothesis direction. Do not
multiply them by direction again. For example, raw -0.4 with direction -1 is reported as +0.4.
Discovery analyses use 95% Welch intervals and need at least 20 observations in every
comparison cell.

Each iteration has explore, analyze, appraise, and synthesize stages. Every stage may register
hypotheses for later analysis. Analyze selects up to 12 previously registered hypotheses.
Appraise assesses every new discovery result, records active/deferred/closed investigation, and may
request validation after considering those results. At most one new voluntary validation request
is allowed per iteration and ten per run. Cached requests reuse the same evidence. The evaluator
may also deliver scheduled validation during the run. Independent intervals account for the maximum
number of validation comparisons in the run. Results arrive before synthesis. Assess newly released
validation immediately in synthesis and explicitly reassess the original claim when its response
deadline appears in the context, even if you also investigate a refinement. The controller maintains
the accepted claim set from your assessments; you do not need to repeat that list. Explanations are
retained for inspection. Acceptance does not require prior independent validation.


You are investigating the supplied research dataset. Return one JSON object using
only this stage's response form. The service performs analyses; you choose the science.
For this task, a relative difference in outcome of 10% or greater is considered clinically significant.
Use your judgment about uncertainty and conclusions in light of this clinical significance threshold. Acceptance does not require
independent validation first. Explain your reasoning in narrative.

The ledger contains every registered claim, its current assessment, and all its available direct
evidence. References H1, H2, ... identify claims; R1, R2, ... identify evidence. Copy these short
references when needed. New proposals receive references automatically after this stage. A changed
comparison or reversed claim is a new proposal, optionally linked to an existing parent.

expectation
of the raw exposed-minus-comparator contrast before seeing evidence (-1, 0 uncertain, +1).
initial_status is your assessment at registration. These initial judgments are recorded once.
If a proposal repeats an existing claim, the controller preserves that claim's current assessment;

For each claim in assessments_due, return one assessment with claim,
status (accept/reject/unresolved),
and investigation (active/deferred/closed). You may also reassess other claims. Omitted claims keep
their current assessment. Assess the original claim even when proposing a refinement or reversal.
By omitting evidence in an assessment, you assess all evidence displayed on that claim's card;
the controller attaches those references. To specify a subset or related evidence, provide evidence
with short R references; include the evidence listed in assessments_due for that claim.
An unchanged assessment or an investigation-only change can use evidence: [];
changing accept/reject/unresolved requires available evidence. Bookkeeping does not satisfy a due
evidence assessment.
For a refinement, parent identifies the earlier claim; omitted motivating_evidence attaches the
parent's displayed evidence. These automatic links record evidence supplied for your assessment
or refinement, not proof that you discussed or understood every result.

The controller maintains the accepted set from your assessments. Do not reconstruct it. Optional
research_notes replaces your persistent notebook; omit it to keep the existing notes. Use it for
plans or reasoning worth retaining. Latest stage narratives are also retained. All earlier numerical
evidence remains in the ledger. Do not repeat completed actions or old responses.
Omit unused fields.

Your action now: Propose scientifically useful new comparisons or refinements for later analysis.

Interpret any new large associations first with strata, marker controls, and possibly one validation if promising.","latest_stage_narratives":{"explore":"Current state: four very large associations are accepted, and three are independently validated in some form: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency is accepted but remains the main large claim without validation. The next exploratory set is therefore weighted toward WRN robustness, independence of co-mutational context for the accepted effects, specificity controls, and a few biologically motivated broad tests that could still clear the clinically meaningful 10% relative benchmark.  \n\nFor WRN, I register refinements asking whether the MSI-high association survives in higher-mutation-burden tumors, in higher-Cas9-activity screens, and in KRAS-wild-type tumors. These address plausible alternatives: that the WRN effect is driven by global hypermutation rather than MSI specifically; that it is an artifact of variable CRISPR quality; or that it is concentrated in a common co-mutational lineage. They complement the pending batch and marker-D controls. If these remain large and controls remain null, they will strengthen the case for independent validation of H6.  \n\nFor SMARCA2, I test SMARCA4 loss among TP53-wild-type tumors to determine whether the effect is not simply entangled with TP53 co-loss. I also add a cross-outcome specificity control: SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A dependency. Because POLR2A is not mechanistically tied to SMARCA4, a near-null result would support outcome-specific paralog dependence, whereas a large effect would raise concern about broader screen or cohort structure affecting SMARCA2.  \n\nFor the validated reversal effects, I test TP53-loss/USP7 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors. KRAS co-mutation is common in lung adenocarcinoma, and these tests ask whether the large associations remain when removing a frequent co-mutational driver context. I also add marker-F controls for USP7 and NFE2L2 because marker-E and marker-D controls are already registered or pending; a null marker-F result would complete a role-free marker control set for these outcomes.  \n\nEGFR amplification remains the most interesting unresolved oncogene match. Its overall point estimate is directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency but small and uncertain. I register an oncogene-exclusive adenocarcinoma context, excluding KRAS mutation, BRAF V600E, and ERBB2 amplification. If EGFR dependency is driven by a cleaner driver-exclusive population, this refinement could clarify whether the small signal becomes clinically meaningful and worth validation.  \n\nFinally, KRAS mutation itself was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency, but pathway dependence may be shaped by upstream regulators. NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling, so I register NF1 loss versus both KRAS and RIT1 dependency. These are exploratory tests of pathway-level dependence after direct KRAS-mutation and STK11-loss tests were not significant. All proposed comparisons remain dataset-specific association tests; none imply causality or external generalizability.","analyze":"The selected 12 analyses are aimed first at the central remaining decision problem: whether the accepted MSI-high/WRN association is robust enough to justify independent validation. If marker-D or one of the technical/co-factor strata shows a large contradictory or attenuating effect, I will defer validation and prioritize confounding explanations.  \n\nThe second block completes marker-D controls for the other accepted very large associations: SMARCA2, NFE2L2, and USP7 (H60, H61, H62). Because research marker D has no assigned biology, a large association would raise concern that the huge dependency-score differences reflect broad correlated cohort or technical structure rather than biomarker-specific association. Near-null marker-D results would strengthen specificity of the accepted effects, especially WRN and SMARCA2.  \n\nI also run H58, the SMARCA4-loss main effect within batch_a, because H50 showed a small opposite batch interaction (R32 -0.051 [-0.095,-0.007]) for SMARCA2. record.narrative: The run now has four large, internally robust, and externally within-dataset validated associations: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency. The next scientific priority is not more validation of those accepted effects, but specificity, context, and broad exploration of previously under-tested outcomes. I therefore defer many small pending refinements, including the EGFR amplification strata and residual accepted-effect subgroup checks, because their existing point estimates are far below the clinically meaningful benchmark or the main effects are already accepted with supporting strata. I closed main broad oncogene nulls H1, H2, and H4 because the central questions have been answered in this dataset. The new hypotheses are designed as falsifiable specificity controls. H77 asks whether TP53 loss also weakens NFE2L2 dependency in the same way KEAP1 loss does; H78 asks whether KEAP1 loss also weakens USP7 dependency in the way TP53 loss does. Large cross-biomarker effects would suggest that the accepted reversal associations are not outcome- or pathway-specific and could reflect broader co-mutational or assay structure, whereas near-null results would strengthen the claim that TP53 loss specifically predicts USP7 dependency and KEAP1 loss specifically predicts NFE2L2 dependency. H79 extends the strong SMARCA4-loss effect to the previously under-tested TMED10 outcome; a large effect would raise concern about broader BAF-related or screen-wide dependency structure, while a null result supports TMED10 specificity and leaves SMARCA2 as the main BAF paralog-associated outcome. H80 tests CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency. CDKN2A loss is a plausible p53-pathway predictor independent of direct TP53 loss, and a clinically meaningful negative raw difference, reflected here as a positive signed estimate under direction -1, would identify a new MDM2 dependency marker. I keep H68 and H76 active as complementary POLR2A specificity controls, H69 and H70 as KRAS-wild-type context checks for the reversal effects, H42 and H47 as marker-E specificity controls, H22 as the existing TMED10 marker control, and H72 as an RAS-pathway exploration of NF1 loss versus RIT1 dependency. All interpretations remain dataset-specific associations, not causal claims or generalizable biological claims.

Study instructions:
Investigate diverse, scientifically meaningful comparisons and use previous
results to allocate further investigation. Broad exploration and focused follow-up are both useful
throughout the run. Assess discoveries in this supplied dataset and use independent validation when
useful. Biological interpretation and generalizability may remain uncertain.

Register comparisons, anticipated directions, and initial assessments before requesting analyses.
The controller assigns claim references. For a changed claim, propose a new comparison and link
refinements to the earlier parent claim.
Clinical log_pfs_months is natural log progression-free survival in months, fully observed without
censoring. Dependency scores are continuous; more negative values mean stronger dependency.
Research signatures are constructed standardized assays in arbitrary units. Research markers D, E,
and F are constructed binary assays with no assigned gene, pathway, or clinical role.
A mean_difference is exposed minus comparator within eligibility and subgroup. An interaction
subtracts that comparison in the subgroup complement in the same eligible population.
Use your scientific judgment to assess the size, uncertainty, and importance of each effect
and decide which conclusions the evidence supports. Explain your reasoning in the narrative.

multiply them by direction again. For example, raw -0.4 with direction -1 is reported as +0.4.
Discovery analyses use 95% Welch intervals and need at least 20 observations in every
comparison cell.

Each iteration has explore, analyze, appraise, and synthesize stages. Every stage may register
hypotheses for later analysis. Analyze selects up to 12 previously registered hypotheses.
Appraise assesses every new discovery result, records active/deferred/closed investigation, and may
request validation after considering those results. At most one new voluntary validation request
is allowed per iteration and ten per run. Cached requests reuse the same evidence. The evaluator
may also deliver scheduled validation during the run. Independent intervals account for the maximum
number of validation comparisons in the run. Results arrive before synthesis. Assess newly released
validation immediately in synthesis and explicitly reassess the original claim when its response
deadline appears in the context, even if you also investigate a refinement. The controller maintains
the accepted claim set from your assessments; you do not need to repeat that list. Explanations are
retained for inspection. Acceptance does not require prior independent validation.


You are investigating the supplied research dataset. Return one JSON object using
only this stage's response form. The service performs analyses; you choose the science.

Use your judgment about uncertainty and conclusions in light of this clinical significance threshold. Acceptance does not require
independent validation first. Explain your reasoning in narrative.

plans or reasoning worth retaining. Latest stage narratives are also retained. All earlier numerical
evidence remains in the ledger. Do not repeat completed actions or old responses.

No causal or external-generalizability claim is made.","latest_stage_narratives":{"explore":"The run now has four large, internally robust, and externally within-dataset validated associations: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency. The next scientific priority is not more validation of those accepted effects, but specificity, context, and broad exploration of previously under-tested outcomes. I therefore defer many small pending refinements, including the EGFR amplification strata and residual accepted-effect subgroup checks, because their existing point estimates are far below the clinically meaningful benchmark or the main effects are already accepted with supporting strata. I closed main broad oncogene nulls H1, H2, and H4 because the central questions have been answered in this dataset. The new hypotheses are designed as falsifiable specificity controls. H77 asks whether TP53 loss also weakens NFE2L2 dependency in the same way KEAP1 loss does; H78 asks whether KEAP1 loss also weakens USP7 dependency in the way TP53 loss does. Large cross-biomarker effects would suggest that the accepted reversal associations are not outcome- or pathway-specific and could reflect broader co-mutational or assay structure, whereas near-null results would strengthen the claim that TP53 loss specifically predicts USP7 dependency and KEAP1 loss specifically predicts NFE2L2 dependency. H79 extends the strong SMARCA4-loss effect to the previously under-tested TMED10 outcome; a large effect would raise concern about broader BAF-related or screen-wide dependency structure, while a null result supports TMED10 specificity and leaves SMARCA2 as the main BAF paralog-associated outcome. H80 tests CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency. CDKN2A loss is a plausible p53-pathway predictor independent of direct TP53 loss, and a clinically meaningful negative raw difference, reflected here as a positive signed estimate under direction -1, would identify a new MDM2 dependency marker. I keep H68 and H76 active as complementary POLR2A specificity controls, H69 and H70 as KRAS-wild-type context checks for the reversal effects, H42 and H47 as marker-E specificity controls, H22 as the existing TMED10 marker control, and H72 as an RAS-pathway exploration of NF1 loss versus RIT1 dependency. If marker-D or one of the technical/co-factor strata shows a large contradictory or attenuating effect, I will defer validation and prioritize confounding explanations.  \n\nThe second block completes marker-D controls for the other accepted very large associations: SMARCA2, NFE2L2, and USP7 (H60, H61, H62). These are dataset-specific association tests; no causal or external-generalizability claim is being advanced.","appraise":"The new WRN evidence strongly supports the already accepted MSI-high association and makes independent validation the highest-value next test. H63 gives a similarly large batch_b main effect, R42 = +0.789 [0.726, 0.852]. These are not small technical artifacts: they are on the order of three standard deviations of the WRN score distribution and far exceed the 10% clinical-significance benchmark under any sensible scale. record.narrative: I select twelve analyses aimed mainly at specificity and broad untested associations rather than additional validation of the four accepted large effects. First, H77 and H78 are cross-biomarker controls: TP53 loss on NFE2L2 dependency and KEAP1 loss on USP7 dependency. Large effects would challenge the outcome specificity of the accepted TP53-USP7 and KEAP1-NFE2L2 associations, while near-null results would strengthen the interpretation that these are selective associations rather than broad consequences of correlated pathway alterations. Second, H79, H68, and H76 are cross-outcome controls on under-tested dependencies: SMARCA4 loss versus TMED10 dependency, SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A dependency, and MSI-high versus POLR2A dependency. Near-null estimates would support that the SMARCA2 and WRN effects are not generic shifts in broad essential dependency or screen structure, whereas large effects would warrant confounding investigations. Third, H42, H47, H74, and H75 complete role-free marker controls for USP7 and NFE2L2 using markers E and F, complementing the null marker-D controls. This tests whether the accepted large reversal effects are tied to assay-agnostic markers. Fourth, H80 tests CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency, a plausible p53-pathway predictor independent of direct TP53 loss. Finally, H72 and H73 test NF1 loss versus RIT1 and KRAS dependency, respectively, because NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling and provides a pathway-level follow-up after direct KRAS mutation was not associated with KRAS dependency. I defer EGFR refinements and KRAS-wild-type context checks for accepted effects this round because EGFR estimates are small and the accepted effects already have strong validation and multiple stratum controls.
